transcript.text: Our Bosch dryer keeps stopping with the empty water container light on but the container is empty?? We've emptied it like 5 times

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. That's a common one, and the light is a bit misleading. On most Bosch condenser and heat-pump dryers it often means "water isn't getting to the container", not "the container needs emptying". The water drips into a sump in the base, a small pump lifts it up to the container, and a float in the base stops the dryer if water builds up down there. 1. Fluff blocking the condenser, sump or pump, so the water can't be lifted.
2. 3. The container isn't being detected, or the float is sticking. 1. Pull the container out, check it isn't cracked and the float or lid is clean, then push it firmly all the way home until it clicks. If the light then clears and stays off, it was just seating.
2. Open the flap at the bottom front and take out the condenser unit, or the second fluff filter on heat-pump models. If it was matted with fluff or water runs out of the base, a blocked path is the likely cause and this may well fix it.
3. Have a look at the back. If a drain hose is fitted (some are plumbed to the sink waste instead of using the container), make sure it isn't kinked or blocked. Then run a normal programme. If it now collects water and runs through, you're sorted. If the container stays bone dry and it stops again, that points to the condensate pump. You can sometimes hear a healthy pump hum briefly during drying, and silence would support a failed pump. Checking the pump usually means taking panels off, so it's often a job for an engineer. To narrow it down: after a run, is there any water at all in the container when you pull it out, or is it completely dry? And when was the condenser (or bottom filter) last cleaned?

I re-seated the container and it clicks in fine, but the light still comes on. The container is nearly empty after a run, just a tiny bit of water in it. I took out the condenser and cleaned it, and it was fairly clean. The little sieve on the container was slimy so I cleaned that too. I can't check the back because it's stacked on the washer with a tower kit, so I can't pull it out. I can't remember when I last cleaned the condenser.

That helps a lot. A tiny bit of water in the container after a full run means the dryer is making condensate but very little of it is reaching the container. The water is being lost or held up somewhere between the sump in the base and the container, so the dryer stops on the warning. 1. Sludge in the path. Fluff and slime in the sump, around the pump inlet or in the small hose up to the container. That slimy sieve is a hint that the same gunk may be further down the line.
2. A weak or failing condensate pump that only manages a trickle.
3. Less likely, the float in the base sticking and triggering the warning falsely. You won't need to move it off the tower for any of these. 1. If the container collects a good amount of water and the light stays off, the slimy sieve was choking the inlet and you're sorted. Clean it every few weeks.
2. While it runs, listen low down at the front every few minutes. A healthy pump usually gives a short hum or gurgle now and then. Silence all the way through points towards the pump.
3. If the light comes back, switch off, unplug, put a towel down and take the condenser out again. Look into the space it sits in. - Water pooled in the base means the water is reaching the sump but not being lifted. That's either a blockage at the pump or the pump itself. - A dry base points more towards the float or the detection.
4. Optional pump test. With the dryer unplugged, carefully pour a glass of water into the base where the condenser sits. Refit everything and run a short programme for 10 to 15 minutes, then check the container. If that water turns up in the container, the pump and hose are working, and the problem is upstream or the float. If it doesn't turn up, the pump or its outlet hose is the likely culprit. If water is sitting in the base and the pump is silent or won't lift that glass of water, the condensate pump is the most likely part. Confirming that and clearing any sludge around it means taking panels off. With the dryer stacked, that's usually best left to an engineer. Let me know what you find after that run.

I took the condenser out again and found a small cover in the base. Behind it was grey slimy water and fluff, so I wiped out what I could reach. It then ran longer, about 60 minutes, but the light came on again. I wouldn't know what the pump should sound like, so I couldn't tell you if it's running. I haven't tried the glass of water thing.

That's real progress. Grey slime and fluff in the base, and the dryer then running longer, tells us the water path was choked. 1. More likely, there's still sludge you couldn't reach, deeper in the pump inlet or in the thin hose that carries water up to the container. The pump can only push a trickle past it.
2. Or the pump itself has got weak, possibly from working against that sludge for a while.
3. Less likely, the float in the base is sticking with slime and triggering the warning even when the level is fine. You don't need to know what the pump sounds like. This test answers it more reliably, and it can all be done from the front with the dryer still on the tower. 1. Switch off and unplug, and put a towel down. Take the condenser out and open that small cover again. Look at whether water has collected in the base since the last stop. If there's a fair amount pooled there, the water is reaching the sump but not being lifted, which points to the pump or its hose.
2. Mop it dry, then slowly pour in about a glass of clean warm water. Watch whether it drains away or just sits there.
3. Refit the cover and condenser, empty the container, plug in and run a short heat programme for 10 to 15 minutes. Then check the container. - Most of the glass turns up in the container: the pump and hose work. The water is more likely being held up elsewhere, or the float is sticking. A careful wipe around the float area in the base is worth doing.
• Only a dribble turns up: there's a partial blockage in the hose or pump inlet, or a weak pump. A couple of warm-water flushes this way sometimes loosens the remaining slime.
• Nothing turns up and the water is still sitting in the base: the condensate pump (or a fully blocked outlet hose) is the most likely culprit. If it points to the pump or a blocked internal hose, sorting it means taking panels off and probably lifting the dryer off the tower. That's a sensible point to get an engineer in. It's normally a fairly modest repair, so it's usually worth doing rather than replacing the dryer. Let me know what the glass of water does.
Ok, I'll give the glass of water test a go and let you know what happens. Just to be clear, I'm doing this from the front only, since I can't pull it off the tower?

Yes, everything in that test is done from the front. You don't need to move the dryer off the tower or touch the back at all. It's just the flap at the bottom, the condenser, that small cover in the base, and the water container at the top. 1. Have it switched off and unplugged while the condenser and cover are out, with a towel on the floor below the flap. The base sits a bit high on a tower, so water can dribble out.
2. Use a jug or a cup with a spout, and pour slowly into the area behind the small cover, so it goes into the sump rather than over the edge.
3. Make sure the cover and condenser are pushed fully back in and locked before you plug in. 4. A short heat programme of 10 to 15 minutes is plenty. Then pull the container out and compare what's in it with what you poured in. What I'm after is roughly how much of that glass turns up: most of it, a dribble, or nothing. Also tell me whether water was already sitting in the base when you opened it up. Those two answers will tell us whether it's leftover sludge in the hose, the pump itself, or the float.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the condenser and water tank are" — On a condenser dryer the water container pulls out at the top and the condenser/heat exchanger sits behind a flap at the bottom front — slide it out and rinse it. Condenser/heat-pump dryers only; layout may differ.]
Ok, thanks, that's clear. I'll do the glass of water test and report back.

No problem, that's the right next step. Just let me know two things when you've done it: roughly how much of the glass ended up in the container (most of it, a dribble, or nothing), and whether there was water already sitting in the base when you opened the cover. If you get the chance, one extra thing is worth noting. The model number (E-Nr) is usually on a label just inside the door rim or on the inside of the bottom flap, both reachable from the front. It isn't essential, but it helps if it does turn out to be the pump.
Ok, will do. I only know from the manual cover that the model starts WTG8, the full label is on the back so I can't read it. I'll report back after the glass of water test.

That's fine, WTG8 is enough for now. That prefix usually means one of Bosch's condenser dryer ranges rather than a heat-pump one, though I can't be certain without the full number. The full number only really matters if it does come down to a part, and an engineer can read it when the dryer comes off the tower. So it's over to the glass of water test. When you report back, the two things I need are how much of the glass turned up in the container (most of it, a dribble, or nothing) and whether water was already sitting in the base when you opened the cover. With those I can tell you whether it's leftover sludge, the pump, or the float.

Container not detected (not fully seated) or a sticking float/level switch (medium)
